summary.text: Set \(M_n=\max_{0\le k\le n}\min\{\binom nk,2^k\}\); the binomial convolution inequality makes \(M_n\) supermultiplicative, so Fekete’s lemma applied to \(-\log M_n\) gives convergence of \(M_n^{1/n}\). At a maximizing index, either its binomial coefficient is already the corresponding residue or maximality makes the next coefficient such a residue; the adjacent-binomial identity then yields \(M_n\le n a(n)\), while termwise bounds give \(a(n)\le nM_n\), and the result follows since \(n^{1/n}\to1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\binom nk\bmod 2^k\right),
\]
where each residue is the least nonnegative residue. We prove that the sequence \(a(n)^{1/n}\) has a finite real limit.

Define the auxiliary sequence
\[
M(n)=\max_{0\le k\le n}\min\!\left\{\binom nk,2^k\right\}.
\]
This maximum exists because the indexing set is finite and nonempty. Notice first that
\[
1\le M(n)\le 2^n. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the term corresponding to \(k=0\) is
\(\min\{\binom n0,2^0\}=1\), proving the lower bound. For every \(k\le n\),
\[
\min\!\left\{\binom nk,2^k\right\}\le 2^k\le 2^n,
\]
which proves the upper bound.

We next show that \(M\) is supermultiplicative:
\[
M(n)M(m)\le M(n+m) \qquad(n,m\ge0). \tag{2}
\]
Choose indices \(k\le n\) and \(j\le m\) at which the maxima defining \(M(n)\) and \(M(m)\) are attained. Thus
\[
M(n)=\min\!\left\{\binom nk,2^k\right\},\qquad
M(m)=\min\!\left\{\binom mj,2^j\right\}.
\]
For nonnegative numbers \(A,B,C,D\),
\[
\min(A,B)\min(C,D)\le \min(AC,BD), \tag{3}
\]
because the left side is at most both \(AC\) and \(BD\). Also, Vandermonde's identity gives
\[
\binom{n+m}{k+j}
 =\sum_{r+s=k+j}\binom nr\binom ms
 \ge \binom nk\binom mj. \tag{4}
\]
Using (3), (4), and \(2^k2^j=2^{k+j}\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
M(n)M(m)
&\le \min\!\left\{\binom nk\binom mj,2^{k+j}\right\}\\
&\le \min\!\left\{\binom{n+m}{k+j},2^{k+j}\right\}\\
&\le M(n+m),
\end{aligned}
\]
since \(k+j\le n+m\). This proves (2).

We now use (2) to prove that the nth roots of \(M(n)\) converge. Put
\[
u(n)=-\log M(n).
\]
All logarithms are defined because \(M(n)\ge1\). From (2) and monotonicity of the logarithm,
\[
\log M(n)+\log M(m)=\log(M(n)M(m))\le \log M(n+m).
\]
After multiplying by \(-1\), this becomes
\[
u(n+m)\le u(n)+u(m), \tag{5}
\]
so \(u\) is subadditive.

Furthermore, the upper bound in (1) implies, for every \(n\ge1\),
\[
\log M(n)\le n\log 2,
\]
and hence
\[
\frac{u(n)}n=-\frac{\log M(n)}n\ge-\log2. \tag{6}
\]
Thus the quotients \(u(n)/n\) are bounded below.

We invoke the standard subadditive form of Fekete's lemma: if a real sequence \(u\) satisfies \(u(r+s)\le u(r)+u(s)\) and the quotients \(u(n)/n\), \(n\ge1\), are bounded below, then they converge to a finite real number, namely
\[
\ell=\inf_{q\ge1}\frac{u(q)}q.
\]
For completeness, the convergence follows by fixing \(q\ge1\) and writing \(n=tq+r\) with \(0\le r<q\). Repeated subadditivity gives
\[
u(n)\le t u(q)+u(r).
\]
For fixed \(q\), the finitely many possible remainder terms \(u(r)\) are bounded above, so division by \(n\) and passage to the upper limit yields
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{u(n)}n\le\frac{u(q)}q.
\]
Taking the infimum over \(q\) gives \(\limsup u(n)/n\le\ell\). By definition of \(\ell\), every quotient is at least \(\ell\), so \(\liminf u(n)/n\ge\ell\). The lower bound (6) ensures that \(\ell\) is finite. Therefore
\[
\frac{u(n)}n\longrightarrow\ell.
\]
Consequently,
\[
M(n)^{1/n}
 =\exp\!\left(\frac{\log M(n)}n\right)
 =\exp\!\left(-\frac{u(n)}n\right)
 \longrightarrow e^{-\ell}. \tag{7}
\]
Denote this positive limit by
\[
L=e^{-\ell}.
\]

It remains to compare \(a(n)\) with \(M(n)\). We shall prove, for every \(n\ge1\),
\[
M(n)\le n\,a(n)\qquad\text{and}\qquad a(n)\le n\,M(n). \tag{8}
\]

The second inequality is immediate. For positive integers \(A,B\), the least nonnegative residue satisfies
\[
A\bmod B\le A,\qquad A\bmod B<B,
\]
and therefore
\[
A\bmod B\le\min(A,B).
\]
Thus, for each \(1\le k\le n\),
\[
\binom nk\bmod 2^k
 \le \min\!\left\{\binom nk,2^k\right\}
 \le M(n).
\]
There are exactly \(n\) summands, so
\[
a(n)\le nM(n). \tag{9}
\]

We now prove the first inequality in (8), which is the main comparison. For \(n=1\), one has \(M(1)=a(1)=1\), so the assertion is clear. Assume henceforth that \(n\ge2\), and choose \(k\), \(0\le k\le n\), such that
\[
M(n)=\min\!\left\{\binom nk,2^k\right\}. \tag{10}
\]
The maximizing index cannot be \(k=0\). Indeed, the value at \(k=0\) is \(1\), whereas the value at \(k=1\) is
\[
\min\!\left\{\binom n1,2\right\}=\min(n,2)=2.
\]
Hence \(M(n)\ge2\), so an index attaining the maximum cannot have value \(1\). Thus
\[
1\le k\le n. \tag{11}
\]

There are two cases.

First suppose
\[
\binom nk<2^k.
\]
Then (10) gives \(M(n)=\binom nk\), and reduction modulo \(2^k\) does nothing:
\[
\binom nk\bmod 2^k=\binom nk=M(n).
\]
Because \(1\le k\le n\), this residue is one of the nonnegative summands in \(a(n)\). Hence
\[
M(n)\le a(n)\le n a(n),
\]
where the last inequality uses \(n\ge1\). This proves the desired bound in the first case.

Now suppose instead that
\[
2^k\le\binom nk. \tag{12}
\]
Then (10) says
\[
M(n)=2^k. \tag{13}
\]
We first note that \(k<n\). If \(k=n\), then (12) would read
\[
2^n\le\binom nn=1,
\]
which is impossible because \(n\ge2\). Therefore \(k+1\le n\).

Maximality at \(k\) now forces
\[
\binom n{k+1}<2^{k+1}. \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, if instead \(2^{k+1}\le\binom n{k+1}\), then the value entering the definition of \(M(n)\) at the index \(k+1\) would be
\[
\min\!\left\{\binom n{k+1},2^{k+1}\right\}=2^{k+1}>2^k=M(n),
\]
contradicting the fact that \(M(n)\) is the maximum.

By (14), the \((k+1)\)-st residue is unreduced:
\[
\binom n{k+1}\bmod 2^{k+1}=\binom n{k+1}.
\]
It is one of the summands of \(a(n)\), so
\[
\binom n{k+1}\le a(n). \tag{15}
\]
We also use the elementary adjacent-binomial identity
\[
\binom n{k+1}(k+1)=\binom nk(n-k). \tag{16}
\]
Since \(k<n\), we have \(n-k\ge1\). Combining (12), (13), and (16),
\[
\begin{aligned}
M(n)
 &=2^k\\
 &\le 2^k(n-k)\\
 &\le \binom nk(n-k)\\
 &=\binom n{k+1}(k+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally, (15) and \(k+1\le n\) imply
\[
\binom n{k+1}(k+1)\le a(n)n.
\]
Therefore \(M(n)\le n a(n)\), completing the second case and the proof of (8).

The lower comparison in (8), together with \(M(n)\ge1\), also shows that \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n\ge1\): otherwise \(n a(n)=0\) could not be at least \(M(n)\ge1\). Thus all of the nth roots below are ordinary positive real roots.

From (8), for \(n\ge1\),
\[
\frac{M(n)}n\le a(n)\le nM(n).
\]
Taking positive nth roots and using multiplicativity of real powers on positive numbers gives
\[
\frac{M(n)^{1/n}}{n^{1/n}}
 \le a(n)^{1/n}
 \le n^{1/n}M(n)^{1/n}. \tag{17}
\]
The classical limit
\[
n^{1/n}\longrightarrow1 \tag{18}
\]
follows, for example, from
\(n^{1/n}=\exp((\log n)/n)\) and \((\log n)/n\to0\).
By (7), \(M(n)^{1/n}\to L\), while (18) shows that both the extra multiplicative factor \(n^{1/n}\) and its reciprocal tend to \(1\). Hence both the lower and upper bounds in (17) tend to \(L\). The squeeze theorem therefore yields
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty}a(n)^{1/n}=L=e^{-\ell}},
\]
where
\[
\ell=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{-\log M(n)}n
     =\inf_{q\ge1}\frac{-\log M(q)}q.
\]
In particular, the asserted limit exists.
